firstAid.title: Pet First Aid Reference
firstAid.subtitle: What you can safely do in the first minutes after an accident — and the warning signs that mean stop and drive to a clinic.

sections.title: Check Airway, Breathing, Circulation
sections.text: Nothing else matters until you know air is moving. Work from the head downwards, and only move the animal if staying put is more dangerous.
bullets: Airway: open the mouth gently and check for vomit, blood or a foreign object.
Breathing: watch the chest for ten seconds — 15 to 35 breaths per minute is normal for dogs and cats.
Circulation: press the gum line; colour should return within two seconds.

sections.title: Control Bleeding
sections.text: Firm direct pressure beats every clever technique. Do not remove clots that have already formed, and avoid tourniquets unless a limb is bleeding uncontrollably.
bullets: Press a clean cloth firmly onto the wound for three minutes without peeking.
Stack more padding on top instead of swapping a soaked dressing.
Elevate the limb only if doing so causes no obvious pain.

sections.title: Support Breathing and CPR
sections.text: Start CPR only when the animal is not breathing and you cannot feel a heartbeat. Work to a rhythm of roughly 30 compressions followed by two rescue breaths.
bullets: Lay the animal on its right side on a firm surface.
Compress the chest 2 to 3 cm deep, around 100 to 120 times per minute.
For rescue breathing, close the mouth and breathe gently until the chest rises.

sections.title: Clear a Choking Airway
sections.text: A choking animal may paw at its mouth, gag or make a high-pitched noise. Only reach inside if you can actually see the object — blind sweeps push it deeper.
bullets: Use a hooked finger only when the item is visible and loose.
Small animals: support the body head-down and give two sharp blows between the shoulder blades.
If it loses consciousness, begin rescue breathing and drive to the clinic.

sections.title: Cool Down Heatstroke
sections.text: Heatstroke kills quickly, but cooling too aggressively is also dangerous. Aim for steady reduction rather than ice.
bullets: Move into shade and wet the body with cool — never ice-cold — water.
Point a fan at the damp fur; the evaporation is what removes heat.
Offer small sips of water and stop active cooling once panting settles.

sections.title: Handle Suspected Poisoning
sections.text: Bring the packaging with you. Treatment depends on the exact substance, and guessing wastes time the animal does not have.
bullets: Never induce vomiting unless a veterinarian tells you to.
Rinse contaminated fur with warm water and mild soap, keeping the animal warm.
Write down the product name, the estimated amount and the time it happened.

sections.title: Prepare for Shock
sections.text: Shock can follow any serious injury. Keep the animal warm, quiet and still, leave the head slightly above the body, and get help — this is not something to treat at home.

checklist.title: Stop treating and drive to a clinic if:
items: Breathing is laboured, noisy, or has stopped.
Bleeding continues after five minutes of firm pressure.
The gums are white, blue or bright red.
The animal has collapsed, is seizing, or cannot stand.
You suspect poisoning, a snake bite or a fall from height.
There is a suspected fracture, or it cannot feel its legs.

firstAid.disclaimer: This reference supports professional veterinary care; it never replaces it. Always call a clinic and describe exactly what you did.
